extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary authors, and informed magazine readers (creative-writers interested in idylls/pastorals and literary criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Distinguish and write idylls vs pastorals; practical advice on composing and presenting rustic/lyrical poetry and on prudent public/political writing. Emphasis on engaging the reader's fancy, economy of verse, and tone/restraint in public prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Idyll'
rubrics_metrics.description: The name properly signifies a poem somewhat rustick in phrase and is descriptive of real scenery and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that an idyll should use a rustic phrase and depict real scenery and manners (contrast with classical dialect questions). Use concrete local detail and realistic rural manners when composing an idyll; the term implies grounded, realistic depiction rather than purely imaginary interlocutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Pastoral'
rubrics_metrics.description: A Pastoral in this context: interlocutors therein are purely imaginary beings and the whole partakes of the nature of a Pastoral rather than a strictly realistic idyll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that the present piece 'does partake of the nature of a Pastoral, inasmuch as the interlocutors therein are purely imaginary beings.' Use this distinction when classifying or composing work: pastorals allow more idealized, interlocutor-driven dialogue and conventions, while idylls emphasize real local detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the reader's fancy fully (don't underestimate the reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There was no greater mistake of an authour than to suppose the reader had no fancy of his own; that, if once that faculty was to be called into activity, it were better to be in for the whole sheep than the shoulder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, call the reader's imaginative faculty into play rather than patronizing it; provide rich stimulus and allow the reader to participate imaginatively. Prefer supplying ample evocative material over withholding or under-describing; trust readers to imagine and complete scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of verse / avoid delaying the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The author relates that some verses were 'stricken out as too much delaying the action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim lyrical or digressive passages that slow narrative momentum. If a passage, however beautiful, stalls the action, consider cutting or tightening it. Use lyrical material to enhance rather than obstruct forward movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading aloud: slow reading with proper emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to 'train to read slowly and with proper emphasis (a practice too much neglected in our modern systems of education)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with performance in mind: craft cadence and emphasis so that prose/poetry can be read aloud slowly and clearly. For writers preparing work for oral presentation, attend to line rhythms, pauses, and emphatic placement to aid expressive reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial humility regarding one's productions
rubrics_metrics.description: An observation that 'we attach a less inordinate value to our own productions' as we age and should 'reconcile ourselves with the wisdom of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate humility about your writing; be open to revision and moderation of self-regard. This affects editorial choices and willingness to excise or revise cherished passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured tone and willingness to admit error in public/political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates the virtue of restraint: 'There are three short and simple words... the hardest of all to pronounce... I was wrong'; 'Let us strengthen the hands of those in authority over us, and curb our own tongues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing on public or political matters, prefer a temperate, conciliatory tone. Admit mistakes plainly when appropriate; avoid maximalist rhetoric that inflames passions. Aim to support constructive authority and to avoid turning public discourse into needless agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible publication: avoid leaking sensitive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning about the pens of others and leaking: 'not to disclose plans... the pens of others, which are swift to convey useful intelligence to the enemy' and historic citation about cautions against publishing military plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and editors should exercise discretion concerning operational or sensitive details that could harm real-world interests. Avoid publishing material that could be exploited by adversaries; balance public interest with responsibility.
